newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian pro-government legislator blasts own party.
newsitem.headline: Russian pro-government legislator blasts own party.

text.p: The parliamentary leader of Russia's main pro-government party said on Thursday its members were confused by the course taken by the cabinet and could not support it without hesitation.

In a sign of turmoil in Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's Our Home is Russia party, Sergei Belyayev, head of the party's deputies in the lower house, said some of its members had voted against a package of government reforms.
He said the government's policies had shifted in the past few months and some deputies were unhappy about it.
"The deputies stick to the party programme but they are under strong pressure to support the government, which now has a quite different programme," he told reporters.
"As a result some of them voted against the cabinet's budget cuts proposals and its social package aimed at slashing welfare benefits."
Chernomyrdin set up his centre-right bloc for a parliamentary election in December 1995. It won solid representation in the State Duma lower house but failed to outnumber the opposition communists.

Major problems emerged after Yeltsin reshaped his government to bring in young reformers, forcing Chernomyrdin, a cautious reformer, to share power with the more radical first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
"Our (the parliamentary group's) position has not only begun to differ from the government's," Belyayev said. "On some issues we occupy quite the opposite position."

The Our Home is Russia parliamentary group stopped short of giving full support to the government proposals to cut budget spending and dump most of the Soviet-era welfare net. These are important parts of the cabinet's economic reform plan.
The Duma rejected the bills and Belyayev said he opposed Chernomyrdin's proposal to summon the chamber for an emergency session later this month to reconsider its decision.
"I think an expensive event such as an extraordinary session of parliament may be held only after government bills are approved by a conciliatory commission," he said.
Chernomyrdin told a meeting of his party's leadership on Tuesday there were tensions inside the party and urged the parliamentary faction to be more cooperative.

Belyayev said the party would have to decide on its future programme at a congress later this year. "Of course there may be a split, because if people think dramatically differently, why should they stay in a single party?" he said.
Chernomyrdin, who will need the party if he decides to stand for president in 2000, also faces problems from another senior member of the parliamentary faction who has spoken out of line.

Lev Rokhlin, head of the Duma's defence committee, said last week that military reform planned by Yeltsin could lead to the complete collapse of the armed forces. Party leaders have criticised Rokhlin but stopped short of ousting him.
